screens.title: Advanced Indexing Strategies and Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn why indexing choices matter beyond simple B-tree indexes. We focus on three specialized index types — geospatial, text, and hashed — and how each maps to specific data models and queries. You will also learn how to read explain output to diagnose slow queries, including which execution stages are red flags and how to compare total keys and documents examined. Index hygiene is a recurring theme: identifying unused or redundant indexes through index statistics prevents wasted disk space and write overhead. We will also explore index cardinality, what makes an index selective, and how cardinality influences query effectiveness. Finally, you’ll consider the operational side: large indexes consume R A M and can increase disk input and output during builds and updates. Throughout the lesson we use concrete examples — a restaurants collection with GeoJSON points, an articles collection with text content, and user/product query patterns — so you can directly apply these strategies. By the end, you’ll be equipped to choose the right index type, interpret explain() output with confidence, and maintain an index set that balances read performance and resource cost.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These four objectives map to practical DBA skills you can apply immediately. First, you will be able to identify and apply specialized indexes — such as geospatial for location data, text for full-text search, and hashed for even sharding — and choose the right one for a given data model. Second, you will master interpreting explain() output so you can spot COLLSCAN, SORT, and other stages and understand why large numbers of keys or documents were examined. Third, you will develop strategies to find unused or redundant indexes using $indexStats and logical analysis, and learn when it’s safe to drop an index. Fourth, you will understand index cardinality and how high or low uniqueness affects selectivity and query performance, and you will consider R A M and disk input and output implications when adding indexes. Each objective includes a short skill description and a simple visual mnemonic to help you remember the approach. Achieving these objectives helps you reduce query latency, lower write overhead, and keep your deployment healthy and scalable.

screens.title: Specialized Index Types — Overview
screens.narratorSegment: Specialized indexes solve specific query patterns that B-tree indexes alone do not handle efficiently. Geospatial indexes, labeled 2dsphere or 2d, are designed for GeoJSON shapes and spherical queries. Use them when documents store coordinates and you need radius, nearest neighbor, or polygon queries. Text indexes power free-text search across one or more string fields and support language processing and stemming; they are ideal for searching article content or product descriptions but have limitations when combined with other operators on the same fields. Hashed indexes store a hash of the field’s value and are primarily useful for evenly distributing documents across shards when used as a shard key; they support equality lookups but not range queries. A common misconception is that hashed indexes always speed up queries — hashed indexes are not a general replacement for B-tree indexes because they only help equality and sharding distribution. A practical scenario: if your application stores GeoJSON points for restaurants, a 2dsphere index enables efficient nearby searches; for blog content, a text index lets users search for keywords. The takeaway is to match the index type to the data shape and the query pattern rather than defaulting to a single index approach.

keyIdea.title: Match index to query
keyIdea.text: Choose geospatial for coordinates, text for keyword search, and hashed for shard distribution or equality-only use.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Specialized Index Types
Definition

Specialized Indexes

Indexes tailored to a data model: geospatial for coordinates, text for free-text search, hashed for sharding and equality lookups.

Geospatial: 2dsphere for GeoJSON points and $near, $geoWithin queries.
Text: full-text search with $text and language-aware features; cannot combine freely with other operators on same fields.
Hashed: stores hashed values for even shard distribution; supports equality only.
Concrete Examples
db.places.createIndex({ location: "2dsphere" })
db.articles.createIndex({ content: "text", title: "text" })
db.users.createIndex({ _id: "hashed" })
Key Takeaway

Specialized indexes exist to match query semantics — use them only when queries require those capabilities.

screens.title: Geospatial Indexes and Queries
screens.narratorSegment: Geospatial queries require data in GeoJSON or legacy coordinate formats and a corresponding spatial index. The most common pattern is a 2dsphere index on a field that stores a GeoJSON Point. When you create db. restaurants. createIndex({ location: '2dsphere' }) you enable queries such as $near and $geoWithin to use spatial operators efficiently. A clear way to validate usage is to run the query with explain('executionStats') and look for geospatial stages such as GEO_NEAR or IXSCAN on the 2dsphere index. A practical example in the hands-on activity creates a restaurants collection with GeoJSON points and then runs a $near query limited by $maxDistance; the explain output should show that the winning plan used the geospatial index. A common misconception is that creating the index alone guarantees fast results; you must also structure the query with GeoJSON geometry and appropriate operators. Another pitfall is forgetting coordinate order: GeoJSON expects [longitude, latitude]. The closing takeaway: ensure your documents use the correct GeoJSON format, build the 2dsphere index, and always confirm explain shows index usage before relying on the query in production. Geospatial Indexes and Queries means create 2dsphere indexes and confirm geo_near or index-backed plan via explain before trusting performance.. In practical terms, create a 2dsphere index and verify geospatial usage with explain. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Geospatial Indexes
Code Walkthrough
Create a restaurants collection and a 2dsphere index, then run a near query with explain to confirm index usage.
use cohortia_restaurants;
db.restaurants.drop();
db.restaurants.insertMany([
  { name: "Taste of Italy", cuisine: "Italian", location: { type: "Point", coordinates: [-73.97, 40.78] } },
  { name: "Sushi Palace", cuisine: "Japanese", location: { type: "Point", coordinates: [-74.00, 40.71] } }
]);
db.restaurants.createIndex({ location: "2dsphere" });

// Then run:
db.restaurants.find({
  location: {
    $near: {
      $geometry: { type: "Point", coordinates: [-73.98, 40.77] },
      $maxDistance: 2000
    }
  }
}).explain("executionStats");
Explanation & Checks
  • Confirm GeoJSON coordinate order is [longitude, latitude].
  • Check explain for GEO_NEAR or an index-backed IXSCAN on the 2dsphere index.
  • If you see COLLSCAN, review document shape and index creation syntax.
Key Takeaway

Index plus correct GeoJSON queries are required; always confirm with explain before deploying.

screens.title: Text Indexes and Limitations
screens.narratorSegment: Text indexes provide language-aware full-text search over string fields by creating term-based entries for searchable text. You can create a text index on one or more fields, for example on title and content, to support keyword searches using the $text operator. Text indexes handle stemming and language-specific rules, which is useful for article or product searches. However, text indexes have specific limitations: they can grow large, they affect disk space and memory usage, and they cannot always be combined with other operators on indexed fields in the same query. A frequent misconception is assuming text indexes behave exactly like dedicated search engines; while they enable many search patterns, they are not a full replacement for specialized search platforms. A concrete example from the chapter creates an articles collection and a text index on title and content, then runs a $text search. Before using text indexes in production, consider size, access patterns, and whether you need more advanced ranking or features offered by search engines. The closing question to reflect on: does your application need language stemming and simple keyword search, or should a dedicated search service be considered?

keyIdea.text: Text indexes enable built-in keyword search but have size and combination limitations; evaluate needs before choosing.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Text Indexes
Concept

Text Index

Create text indexes on string fields to enable $text searches with language support and stemming. Use them where keyword search over documents is required.

use cohortia_articles;
db.articles.drop();
db.articles.insertMany([
  { title: "MongoDB Performance Tips", content: "Learn how to optimize your MongoDB queries with indexes and aggregation." },
  { title: "Node.js Best Practices", content: "Explore asynchronous programming and error handling in Node.js applications." }
]);
db.articles.createIndex({ title: "text", content: "text" });

// Search:
db.articles.find({ $text: { $search: "MongoDB queries" } }).explain("executionStats");
Limitations & Misconceptions
  • Text indexes can be large and consume disk/memory. Plan capacity accordingly.
  • You cannot freely combine $text on indexed fields with other operators on the same fields in the same query in some cases.
  • Text indexes are not a replacement for advanced search engines if ranking and complex queries are required.
Key Takeaway

Use text indexes for built-in keyword searches, but evaluate size and query combination limits before adoption.

screens.title: Hashed Indexes and Sharding
screens.narratorSegment: Hashed indexes compute a hash value from the field and index that hash rather than the original value. Their main role in practice is to serve as a shard key to evenly distribute documents across shards, which helps avoid hot spots when the original field has monotonically increasing values. Hashed indexes support equality matches but are not useful for range queries because hashing destroys order. This makes them less helpful for general query optimization compared to B-tree compound or single-field indexes. A common mistake is assuming a hashed index will speed up range-based queries or sort operations. Instead, use hashed indexes when your primary goal is distribution for sharding and your query patterns rely on equality. An example from the chapter is creating a hashed index on _id for sharding: db. users. createIndex({ _id: 'hashed' }). The takeaway is clear: prefer hashed for shard uniformity and equality lookups, and prefer B-tree indexes for sorts, ranges, and compound predicate coverage. Hashed Indexes and Sharding means use hashed indexes primarily for sharding and equality; they do not support range queries or ordered scans.. In practical terms, why hashed indexes exist and their practical constraints. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Hashed Indexes
Definition

Hashed Index

Indexes a hash of field values. Useful for shard keys and equalities; not suitable for ordered or range queries.

db.users.createIndex({ _id: "hashed" })
Practical Notes
  • Choose hashed when distributing writes and avoiding monotonic hot shards is a priority.
  • Do not expect hashed indexes to aid range queries or provide sort order.
  • For query optimization that requires ordering or ranges, prefer compound B-tree indexes.
Key Takeaway

Pick hashed indexes for shard distribution and equality; use B-tree for range and sort needs.

screens.title: Using explain() to Diagnose Slow Queries
screens.narratorSegment: Explain is your primary diagnostic tool for slow queries. When you run explain('executionStats') you get an execution plan and counts that tell you how work was performed. The most common red flag is stage: COLLSCAN — a full collection scan — which usually means you need an index or the wrong index is being used. Another issue is SORT or SORT_KEY_GENERATOR appearing without a covering IXSCAN; that indicates MongoDB performed an in-memory sort because no index provided the required order. Pay close attention to totalDocsExamined, totalKeysExamined, and nReturned. Ideally, totalKeysExamined should be close to nReturned when the index filters precisely; if totalDocsExamined is much larger than nReturned you have a broad scan that filters out many documents after retrieval. If totalKeysExamined is much larger than nReturned, the index scan is scanning many entries to find few matches. Also check winningPlan. queryPlanner. indexFilterSet to know whether index filters restricted the optimizer. A common misconception is blaming application code rather than inspecting the plan; start with explain and compare counts to understand whether you need different indexes, a different index order, or query rewrite. The final question: does the plan show an index doing the heavy lifting or is MongoDB still scanning too many records?

keyIdea.title: Explain checklist
keyIdea.text: Look for COLLSCAN, SORT without IXSCAN, and compare totalDocsExamined vs totalKeysExamined vs nReturned to identify inefficiencies.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Explain() Diagnosis
Step-by-step Checks
  1. Stage Check: Watch for COLLSCAN as a red flag.
  2. Sort Check: SORT or SORT_KEY_GENERATOR without IXSCAN implies in-memory sorting.
  3. Counts Check: Compare totalDocsExamined, totalKeysExamined, and nReturned for selectivity.
  4. Index Filter: Inspect winningPlan.queryPlanner.indexFilterSet to see index restrictions.
Concrete Example
Using the products collection with an index { category: 1, price: -1 }, run explain on a sorted query and compare two explain outputs: one efficient and one less efficient. The difference in totalDocsExamined reveals selectivity problems.
Common Mistake

Assuming an index exists means the query is efficient; confirm via explain counts and stages instead.

screens.title: Understanding Keys vs Documents Examined
screens.narratorSegment: Interpreting totalKeysExamined and totalDocsExamined is essential for diagnosing why a query remains slow. totalKeysExamined counts how many index entries MongoDB scanned; totalDocsExamined counts how many documents it inspected. For an efficient index-backed query, totalKeysExamined should be close to nReturned because the index directly points to matching documents. If totalKeysExamined is very high relative to nReturned, the index scan is broad and not selective — perhaps due to poor key ordering or a non-selective leading field. If totalDocsExamined is much larger than nReturned, it means MongoDB fetched many documents that were later filtered out by predicates that the index did not cover; this often happens when range predicates are applied on fields not ordered properly in the index. Consider the example from the chapter: a category filter with a price sort. One explain shows low examined counts when the compound index { category: 1, price: -1 } is present and ordered correctly; another query using regex on category causes many documents to be examined. A misconception to avoid is treating totalKeysExamined alone as sufficient; always compare both counts and nReturned to get the full picture. The practical step: change index ordering or add the range field to the compound index so the index can filter before document fetch.

keyIdea.title: Counts tell the story
keyIdea.text: Compare keys and docs examined against nReturned to determine whether an index narrows the search effectively or only scans broadly.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Keys vs Docs
Efficient Case

When totalKeysExamined ≈ nReturned and totalDocsExamined is low, the index is selective and doing most of the work.

Desired: totalKeysExamined close to nReturned
Inefficient Case

If totalDocsExamined >> nReturned, many documents were fetched then filtered. If totalKeysExamined >> nReturned, the index scan is too broad.

Problem patterns: broad leading index fields or missing range field in compound index
Concrete Example
// Efficient index:
db.products.createIndex({ category: 1, price: -1 });
db.products.find({ category: "Category 50" }).sort({ price: -1 }).explain("executionStats");

// Less efficient if category is broad or regex is used:
db.products.find({ category: { $regex: "^Category 5" } }).sort({ price: -1 }).explain("executionStats");

screens.title: Index Filter Set and the Query Planner
screens.narratorSegment: The query planner evaluates candidate indexes and chooses a winning plan. One element you may see in explain output is winningPlan. queryPlanner. indexFilterSet, which indicates whether an index filter was applied to limit the optimizer’s choices. Index filters can be used to force or recommend certain indexes during tuning, but they can also mask better plans if used incorrectly. When troubleshooting, you should first inspect the planner without index filters to see the natural selection. If an index filter is present, confirm it was intentional and that it narrows the optimizer in a beneficial way. A misconception is assuming the planner always picks the best plan in all contexts; sometimes planner heuristics and historical statistics lead to suboptimal choices, and an index filter is a tuning tool to correct that. However, use filters sparingly and monitor effects. The practical workflow: run explain without filters, observe stages and counts, then consider index filters only as a last resort after validating index design and query shape. The closing question: are you changing planner behavior or fixing the underlying index/query mismatch? Index Filter Set and the Query Planner means index filters restrict optimizer choices; use them only after validating native planner decisions and index designs.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. narration.text: The query planner evaluates candidate indexes and chooses a winning plan. One element you may see in explain output is winningPlan. queryPlanner. indexFilterSet, which indicates whether an index filter was applied to limit the optimizer’s choices. When troubleshooting, you should first inspect the planner without index filters to see the natural selection. If an index filter is present, confirm it was intentional and that it narrows the optimizer in a beneficial way. A misconception is assuming the planner always picks the best plan in all contexts; sometimes planner heuristics and historical statistics lead to suboptimal choices, and an index filter is a tuning tool to correct that. However, use filters sparingly and monitor effects. What indexFilterSet Means

If indexFilterSet is true, an index filter limited the planner’s candidate indexes. This can be a deliberate tuning step or an accidental restriction.

  • Check planner output without filters first.
  • Use filters only when you’ve proven the planner chooses worse plans under production patterns.
Practical Tip

Temporarily remove filters in a staging environment and compare explain counts. If filters improve stability across known queries, document and monitor them closely.

Common Mistake

Relying on index filters to hide a poor index design rather than fixing index order or selectivity.

screens.title: Identify and Manage Unused or Redundant Indexes
screens.narratorSegment: Index bloat harms write performance and consumes disk and memory. Detecting unused or redundant indexes is a continuous maintenance activity. Start by running $indexStats on each index and review accesses. ops over an appropriate timeframe. An index with zero accesses is a candidate for removal, but always cross-check against known application queries and seasonal usage patterns. Redundant indexes arise when a more specific compound index covers a less specific single-field index; for example, { a: 1, b: 1 } can make { a: 1 } redundant for queries that can use the compound index. Before dropping an index, verify the queries that rely on it and ensure replica set or backup strategies protect you if you must roll back. A misconception is to remove indexes solely on short-term statistics; combine $indexStats with query logs and explain outputs. The practical workflow: collect $indexStats, map indexes to query patterns, identify zero or low access indexes, test removing in staging, and then schedule removal in production during a maintenance window. The final question: does each index justify its ongoing write and storage cost?

Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Index Hygiene
Workflow
  1. Collect $indexStats and sort by accesses.ops over your monitoring window.
  2. Map each index to active query patterns and explain outputs.
  3. Flag zero or low-access indexes for staging removal tests.
  4. Schedule safe removal during maintenance if tests pass.
Redundancy Example

An index on { a: 1, b: 1 } can make { a: 1 } redundant for many queries — validate query coverage before dropping the single-field index.

Key Takeaway

Prune indexes with evidence: combine $indexStats, query logs, and explain output before removal.

screens.title: Index Cardinality and Selectivity
screens.narratorSegment: Index cardinality is the count of unique values in an indexed field relative to the total documents. High cardinality — many unique values like an email or _id — makes indexes highly selective and effective because queries quickly narrow to a small subset. Low cardinality — few distinct values like status or gender — often yields poor selectivity on its own and might be inefficient unless combined in a compound index or used with partial indexes. A typical misconception is that any indexed field is helpful; in reality, an index on a boolean or highly skewed field can increase overhead without improving query performance. The best practice is to evaluate cardinality and use low-cardinality fields in compound indexes after a more selective leading field, or consider partial indexes if only a subset of values is frequently queried. For example, indexing a boolean where 99% of documents are true yields little benefit. The practical takeaway: measure distinct value counts, estimate selectivity, and design compound indexes following equality-then-range ordering to maximize usefulness. keyIdea.text: High cardinality yields selectivity; low cardinality should be combined in compound or partial indexes for effectiveness.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Cardinality & Selectivity
What is Cardinality?

The number of distinct values in an indexed field. High cardinality increases selectivity and index usefulness; low cardinality reduces it.

Example: email (high) vs status boolean (low)
Design Guidance
  • Place equality fields first in compound indexes, then range or sort fields.
  • Combine low-cardinality fields with selective leading fields or use partial indexes.
  • Estimate distinct counts before adding single-field indexes on low-cardinality data.
Key Takeaway

Measure uniqueness before indexing; design compound indexes to amplify selectivity.

screens.title: Operational Impact: RAM and Disk I/O
screens.narratorSegment: Indexes are not free. They consume disk space permanently and use R A M for frequently accessed portions. Large index sets increase memory pressure and can lead to higher disk input and output during index builds and when updating indexed fields. In write-heavy workloads, every index adds overhead because writes must update all relevant index structures, increasing latency and input and output. In a sharded cluster, index choices also affect shard key behavior and distribution. A common operational mistake is accumulating many low-value indexes that slow writes and consume memory without improving reads. The safer approach is to balance read improvements against write cost: keep only indexes that serve important queries, use partial indexes for targeted coverage, and schedule index builds during maintenance windows to avoid high input and output. Monitor R A M usage and input and output patterns during index builds and under normal operation to ensure you are not swapping or causing frequent disk reads. The final reflective question: does this index reduce query latency enough to justify the ongoing memory and input and output cost? content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › RAM & Disk I/O
Why Indexes Affect Resources
  • Indexes occupy disk space and may be partially or wholly resident in RAM depending on activity.
  • Index builds and updates generate disk I/O; many indexes amplify this effect during writes.
  • High memory pressure can cause swapping and degrade performance; monitor server metrics when changing indexes.
Practical Strategies
  1. Prune unused indexes to reduce write amplification and storage.
  2. Build large indexes during maintenance windows to minimize impact.
  3. Consider partial indexes to cover only frequently queried subsets of data.
Key Takeaway

Weigh indexing benefit against RAM and I/O cost; prefer targeted indexes and scheduled builds for large datasets.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Here are the core concepts to keep in mind. First, pick the index that matches your data and queries: 2dsphere for GeoJSON points and spatial queries, text for keyword searches across string fields, and hashed indexes when you need even shard distribution for equality. Second, use explain('executionStats') to diagnose performance: watch for COLLSCAN and SORT without an index, and compare totalKeysExamined, totalDocsExamined, and nReturned to assess selectivity. Third, maintain index hygiene by using $indexStats to find unused indexes and by recognizing when compound indexes make single-field indexes redundant. Fourth, cardinality determines selectivity — high cardinality is usually better for single-field indexes; low-cardinality fields often belong in compound or partial indexes. Finally, remember the resource trade-offs: each index increases disk usage and write input and output and can add memory pressure. Keep these principles together when designing and maintaining indexes to balance query speed with system cost.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn why indexing choices matter beyond simple B-tree indexes. We focus on three specialized index types — geospatial, text, and hashed — and how each maps to specific data models and queries. You will also learn how to read explain output to diagnose slow queries, including which execution stages are red flags and how to compare total keys and documents examined. Index hygiene is a recurring theme: identifying unused or redundant indexes through index statistics prevents wasted disk space and write overhead. We will also explore index cardinality, what makes an index selective, and how cardinality influences query effectiveness. Finally, you’ll consider the operational side: large indexes consume R A M and can increase disk input and output during builds and updates. Throughout the lesson we use concrete examples — a restaurants collection with GeoJSON points, an articles collection with text content, and user/product query patterns — so you can directly apply these strategies. By the end, you’ll be equipped to choose the right index type, interpret explain() output with confidence, and maintain an index set that balances read performance and resource cost.

These four objectives map to practical DBA skills you can apply immediately. First, you will be able to identify and apply specialized indexes — such as geospatial for location data, text for full-text search, and hashed for even sharding — and choose the right one for a given data model. Second, you will master interpreting explain() output so you can spot COLLSCAN, SORT, and other stages and understand why large numbers of keys or documents were examined. Third, you will develop strategies to find unused or redundant indexes using $indexStats and logical analysis, and learn when it’s safe to drop an index. Fourth, you will understand index cardinality and how high or low uniqueness affects selectivity and query performance, and you will consider R A M and disk input and output implications when adding indexes. Each objective includes a short skill description and a simple visual mnemonic to help you remember the approach. Achieving these objectives helps you reduce query latency, lower write overhead, and keep your deployment healthy and scalable.

This screen translates each objective into a concrete action you can practice. For specialized indexes, create a 2dsphere on a restaurants collection and run a near query to see GEO_NEAR or similar in explain output. For explain() analysis, run explain('executionStats') on slow queries and compare totalKeysExamined, totalDocsExamined and nReturned to judge selectivity and efficiency. For index hygiene, gather $indexStats and look for indexes with zero or very low accesses over a relevant timeframe before planning removal. For cardinality and resource impact, evaluate the uniqueness of a field and simulate load: high-cardinality fields like email benefit single-field indexes, whereas low-cardinality fields work best inside compound indexes or as partial indexes. Each action is deliberately measurable so you can verify the effect on query latency and resource metrics. Practicing these steps will make index decisions evidence-based rather than guesswork.

Specialized indexes solve specific query patterns that B-tree indexes alone do not handle efficiently. Geospatial indexes, labeled 2dsphere or 2d, are designed for GeoJSON shapes and spherical queries. Use them when documents store coordinates and you need radius, nearest neighbor, or polygon queries. Text indexes power free-text search across one or more string fields and support language processing and stemming; they are ideal for searching article content or product descriptions but have limitations when combined with other operators on the same fields. Hashed indexes store a hash of the field’s value and are primarily useful for evenly distributing documents across shards when used as a shard key; they support equality lookups but not range queries. A common misconception is that hashed indexes always speed up queries — hashed indexes are not a general replacement for B-tree indexes because they only help equality and sharding distribution. A practical scenario: if your application stores GeoJSON points for restaurants, a 2dsphere index enables efficient nearby searches; for blog content, a text index lets users search for keywords. The takeaway is to match the index type to the data shape and the query pattern rather than defaulting to a single index approach.

Geospatial queries require data in GeoJSON or legacy coordinate formats and a corresponding spatial index. The most common pattern is a 2dsphere index on a field that stores a GeoJSON Point. When you create db. restaurants. createIndex({ location: '2dsphere' }) you enable queries such as $near and $geoWithin to use spatial operators efficiently. A clear way to validate usage is to run the query with explain('executionStats') and look for geospatial stages such as GEO_NEAR or IXSCAN on the 2dsphere index. A practical example in the hands-on activity creates a restaurants collection with GeoJSON points and then runs a $near query limited by $maxDistance; the explain output should show that the winning plan used the geospatial index. A common misconception is that creating the index alone guarantees fast results; you must also structure the query with GeoJSON geometry and appropriate operators. Another pitfall is forgetting coordinate order: GeoJSON expects [longitude, latitude]. The closing takeaway: ensure your documents use the correct GeoJSON format, build the 2dsphere index, and always confirm explain shows index usage before relying on the query in production. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Text indexes provide language-aware full-text search over string fields by creating term-based entries for searchable text. You can create a text index on one or more fields, for example on title and content, to support keyword searches using the $text operator. A concrete example from the chapter creates an articles collection and a text index on title and content, then runs a $text search. Hashed indexes compute a hash value from the field and index that hash rather than the original value.
